description: Registry of the recurring research releases jobsdata.ai tracks. Powers /data-sources and future auto-ingest workflows.

series.name: Employment Situation (Jobs Report)
series.releasePattern: First Friday of each month, 8:30am ET
series.topicLine: The headline US jobs report — nonfarm payrolls and unemployment rate.
series.whatItMeasures: Net change in nonfarm payroll employment and the unemployment rate, from two Census-run surveys (~119K businesses and ~60K households). Broken out by industry, age, race, and education.
series.whyItMatters: The single most-cited labor market signal. AI's aggregate effect (or lack thereof) shows up here first if it's happening at scale. Prior-month revisions often reveal that early estimates over- or under-stated the trend.

lastIngested.value: +57K nonfarm; U-rate 4.2%; Apr/May revised -74K

series.name: Challenger Job Cuts Report (with AI attribution)
series.releasePattern: First Thursday of each month
series.topicLine: Employer-announced layoffs with a specific 'AI-attributed' category.
series.whatItMeasures: Job-cut announcements tracked from public sources, self-reported employer rationale, and Challenger's outreach. Uniquely tags cuts where AI is named as the driver.
series.whyItMatters: The most-cited source when the media reports 'AI-driven layoffs.' Signal is early but noisy — attribution reflects what employers say publicly, which may over- or under-state AI's actual role.

lastIngested.value: ~102K AI-attributed job cuts YTD; tech = 1/3 of announcements

series.name: Ramp AI Economics Velocity
series.releasePattern: Ad hoc; typically monthly on ramp.com/velocity
series.topicLine: Firm-level AI spend and hiring signals from Ramp's business-card data.
series.whatItMeasures: Aggregated spend and hiring patterns across ~30K businesses using Ramp's expense/card platform. Provides one of the fastest reads on firm AI-tool adoption and its correlation with hiring behavior.
series.whyItMatters: Fills the gap between quarterly earnings and monthly BLS — private data with a real-time cadence. Ramp's finding that AI-intensive firms are adding jobs faster than laggards is a key counter to the displacement narrative.

lastIngested.value: AI-intensive firms adding jobs faster than laggards

series.name: Fed Reserve — Monitoring AI Adoption in the US Economy
series.releasePattern: FEDS Notes format; typically every 3-4 months
series.topicLine: Official Fed synthesis of the many US AI-adoption survey series.
series.whatItMeasures: Reconciles BTOS, ADP, NY Fed SCE, and academic-tracker series to produce the Fed's own reading of firm and worker AI adoption trends.
series.whyItMatters: One of the very few sources that formally reconciles disagreements between adoption surveys. Fed's involvement lends institutional weight to whatever the current best estimate is.

lastIngested.value: Broader synthesis of BTOS + ADP + SCE

series.name: Census Business Trends & Outlook Survey — AI Supplement
series.releasePattern: Alternating Thursdays
series.topicLine: The freshest firm-side AI adoption measure available in the US.
series.whatItMeasures: The share of ~1.2M US businesses that report using AI in the past two weeks. Broken out by sector, state, and the 25 largest MSAs. Question wording revised in Nov 2025 to include 'any business function' (up from the narrower 'production of goods and services' framing), roughly doubling the measured rate.
series.whyItMatters: Highest-frequency US firm-level adoption signal. Because it's biweekly, it reveals turn-of-quarter shifts that quarterly surveys miss. Adoption still concentrated in Information (39.7%) and Finance (33.9%).

lastIngested.value: 17.9% national AI use (Q1 2-wk); GenAI at work 20.8%; task substitution 10.1%

series.nextExpected: ~Q3 2026 biweekly wave; next full AI Supplement ~Q1 2027

series.name: FactSet S&P 500 Earnings Call AI Mentions
series.releasePattern: Published mid-way through each S&P 500 reporting season (~Feb, May, Aug, Nov)
series.topicLine: How often S&P 500 companies mention 'AI' on their quarterly earnings calls.
series.whatItMeasures: The percentage of S&P 500 companies whose earnings call transcripts include the term 'AI.' Reported quarterly with an interim update after ~50% of companies have reported.
series.whyItMatters: The clearest cadence-consistent read of corporate AI focus. Q4 2025 hit an all-time high (68%); Q1 2026's slight dip to 65% was the first sequential decline in the ChatGPT era.

lastIngested.value: 65% of S&P 500 calls cited AI (down from 68% Q4 2025)

series.name: GenAI Adoption Tracker (Bick, Blandin, Deming RPS)
series.publisher: St. Louis Fed / Harvard (Real-Time Population Survey)
series.releasePattern: Roughly every 3 months at genaiadoptiontracker.com
series.topicLine: The definitive quarterly measure of US worker generative AI adoption.
series.whatItMeasures: Share of US adults 18-64 using generative AI (a) overall and (b) at work. Fielded quarterly via the Real-Time Population Survey (RPS), which has published its GenAI module every 3 months since August 2024.
series.whyItMatters: The single cleanest time series on worker-side GenAI adoption in the US, cited by every major synthesis (Stanford DEL, IMF, Fed, OECD). Nationally representative and cadence-consistent.

lastIngested.value: 45.2% of US workers use GenAI for work (up from 43% Feb 2026)

series.name: Yale Budget Lab — Tracking AI's Impact on the Labor Market
series.releasePattern: Each new CPS release; typically monthly commentary, quarterly deep-dives
series.topicLine: The main counter-evidence to the ADP 'Canaries' finding — no aggregate AI-labor effect visible in CPS.
series.whatItMeasures: Uses the Current Population Survey to test whether AI-exposed occupations are seeing employment declines. Complements the ADP-based Canaries with a different dataset and a different unit of analysis.
series.whyItMatters: The Yale team's 'no effect yet' reading disciplines the field — anyone claiming AI-driven displacement has to reconcile with CPS data that doesn't show it. Their published disagreements with Stanford DEL are among the most important debates in the field.

lastIngested.value: AI 'probably not (yet)' the reason for labor market weakening

series.name: Stanford DEL — AI Economic Indicators (Canaries + Takeoff + Adoption)
series.releasePattern: Research notes ~quarterly; dashboards update monthly at digitaleconomy.stanford.edu
series.topicLine: Three linked dashboards: employment by age × AI exposure, macro takeoff signals, and worker adoption.
series.whatItMeasures: Canaries Dashboard tracks employment across 5-year balanced ADP payroll sample (25K firms, 4.6M workers). Takeoff Tracker follows 12 macro indicators for AI-driven growth. Adoption Monitor synthesizes surveys.
series.whyItMatters: The Canaries finding — early-career workers 22-25 in most-exposed occupations contracting -3.8%/yr — is the most-cited AI-displacement evidence in the field. Takeoff Tracker's 7-no / 3-mild / 2-strong reading is the field's best macro summary.

lastIngested.value: Canaries: -3.8%/yr early-career in most-exposed; Takeoff: no decisive evidence

series.nextExpected: Dashboards refresh monthly; next research note ~September 2026

series.name: Anthropic Economic Index (Learning Curves, Cadences)
series.releasePattern: Themed reports every ~3 months on anthropic.com/research
series.topicLine: How Claude.ai users actually work with AI — the largest usage dataset in the field.
series.whatItMeasures: Analyzes millions of Claude conversations to classify task types (automation vs augmentation), occupation coverage, and skill-formation effects. Each report covers a themed angle: economic primitives, learning curves, cadences, etc.
series.whyItMatters: The only source that grounds AI-labor claims in actual usage data at scale. Automation-ratio findings (used by Stanford DEL's Canaries analysis) have become a field standard for measuring 'how AI is being used' at the occupation level.

lastIngested.value: 50% say Claude handles 50%+ of tasks; 4% say entire job

series.name: PwC AI Jobs Barometer
series.releasePattern: Once per year, typically ~June, with interim country updates
series.topicLine: The largest job-postings-based analysis of AI's labor market impact — 1B+ ads across 27 countries.
series.whatItMeasures: Analyzes 1B+ job advertisements across 27 countries plus company financial and O*NET task data. Reports AI-skill wage premium, 'seniorised' entry-level shifts, and productivity growth by AI exposure.
series.whyItMatters: The largest cross-country postings analysis. The 2026 edition's 'seniorisation' finding — entry-level roles 7x more likely to need senior skills — has reframed how the field talks about early-career displacement.

lastIngested.value: 62% AI-skill wage premium; seniorised entry-level +35% since 2019 vs -10% others

series.name: NY Fed Survey of Consumer Expectations — AI Module
series.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
series.releasePattern: Rolling ~quarterly special-topic releases at libertystreeteconomics.newyorkfed.org
series.topicLine: Worker-side self-reported AI use and training access, from the NY Fed's household panel.
series.whatItMeasures: Household survey covering ~1,300 US workers on AI-tool use at work, employer-provided training, and perceived job-security effects. Published as themed Liberty Street Economics posts.
series.whyItMatters: One of the few sources measuring not just adoption but access to employer training on AI — where the divides (income, education, race) are widening fastest. April 2026 report: only 15.9% of employers offer AI training; 38% of workers want it.

lastIngested.value: Only 15.9% of employers offer AI training; 37% of workplaces don't offer AI tools

series.name: Gallup Workplace AI Adoption Tracking
series.releasePattern: Themed workplace reports every ~3 months at gallup.com/workplace
series.topicLine: Large-sample worker-side AI adoption and sentiment, from Gallup's employed-adult panel.
series.whatItMeasures: Surveys of 20K+ US employees on AI use frequency, workplace attitudes, productivity perceptions, and industry-specific reports (arts/creative most recently).
series.whyItMatters: The largest single-survey read of US worker AI adoption (Feb 2026 sample: 23,717). Frequency breakdown (13% daily / 28% weekly+ / 50% at-least-annually) is more granular than most trackers.

lastIngested.value: AI in creative work — arts sector deep-dive

series.name: Ellucian Annual Higher Education AI Survey
series.releasePattern: March each year
series.topicLine: The main annual measure of higher-ed AI adoption and workforce impact.
series.whatItMeasures: Surveys ~779 higher-ed faculty and administrators from 300+ US institutions on institutional AI adoption, use cases, and workforce effects.
series.whyItMatters: Highest-cadence-consistent read of higher-ed AI. 3rd edition (Mar 2026) found 66% of institutions using AI (up from 49% YoY) — one of the steepest year-on-year jumps in any sector.

lastIngested.value: 66% of higher-ed institutions using AI (up from 49% YoY)

series.name: EDUCAUSE Higher Ed IT Workforce Report
series.releasePattern: Late spring / early summer
series.topicLine: How higher-ed IT teams are adapting to AI, budget pressure, and strategic change.
series.whatItMeasures: Surveys higher-ed IT professionals on workforce composition, AI-driven role changes, budget dynamics, and burnout. The 2026 edition explicitly named AI adaptation as a top-3 workforce pressure.
series.whyItMatters: Complements Ellucian by focusing specifically on the IT-professional workforce inside higher-ed — the fastest-changing job family in the sector.

lastIngested.value: AI + budget pressure + strategic change as top-3 pressures on higher-ed IT teams

series.name: Metaculus AI Labor Automation Forecasting Hub
series.publisher: Metaculus / Renaissance Philanthropy / Schultz Family Foundation
series.releasePattern: Real-time updating as forecasters submit predictions
series.topicLine: Community forecasts on AI-related employment changes by 2030.
series.whatItMeasures: Structured forecast questions (probability distributions) on occupation-level employment changes through 2030 across ~50 major US occupations. Median community estimates update continuously.
series.whyItMatters: The only source giving quantitative 5-year forecasts by occupation. Latest reads: software developers -15.1%, CS/sales reps -11%, financial specialists -8.1%, lawyers -5.4%.

lastIngested.value: Software developers -15.1%; CS/sales -11%; K-12 teachers +1.3% by 2030

series.nextExpected: Continuous; check quarterly for shifts in community medians

series.name: Census Business Formation Statistics
series.releasePattern: Second Wednesday of each month
series.topicLine: The official US count of new business applications and formations.
series.whatItMeasures: New business applications (any) and high-propensity applications (likely to become employer businesses), by state, industry, and month.
series.whyItMatters: The universe-scale ground truth on US business formation. AI's role is inferred from sectoral patterns (professional services growing 4x faster than construction since ChatGPT) rather than directly tagged.

lastIngested.value: 531,423 business applications (+1.1% MoM); 29,741 projected formations

series.name: WEF Future of Jobs Report
series.releasePattern: January of odd years (typically ahead of Davos)
series.topicLine: The largest employer-side survey on jobs and skills through the AI transition.
series.whatItMeasures: Surveys 1,000+ large employers globally on hiring, displacement, reskilling, and skill demand over the following 5 years. Reports at country, industry, and role level.
series.whyItMatters: The most-cited employer-side projection. 2025 edition projected 92M roles displaced by 2030 offset by 170M created (net +78M). Sector-specific projections widely used in policy planning.

lastIngested.value: 92M roles displaced by 2030; 170M created; net +78M

series.name: OECD.AI Observatory & Employment Outlook AI chapters
series.cadenceLabel: Rolling; annual Employment Outlook + AI-specific interim reports
series.releasePattern: Rolling updates at oecd.ai; annual OECD Employment Outlook (typically July)
series.topicLine: The only cross-country AI-adoption and AI-labor comparator on the registry.
series.whatItMeasures: AI adoption by firms, workers, and countries across OECD members (currently 38 nations). Combines Eurostat firm-side data, ISCO occupational exposure, PIAAC skills, and country-level policy indicators into the OECD.AI Index. Employment Outlook chapters add the annual synthesis.
series.whyItMatters: US-only findings need a cross-country test. The Bick/Blandin/Deming RPS series and Humlum/Vestergaard's Danish study are only interpretable against this comparator. OECD 2026 shows Denmark at 42% firm adoption vs US at 17% — the cleanest evidence that adoption isn't only about model availability.

lastIngested.value: OECD 2026 Employment Outlook: AI and trade reshape regional labor markets; Denmark 42% firm AI, US 17%

series.name: NBER Working Papers — AI & Labor
series.cadenceLabel: Weekly release cadence; monthly for the AI-labor subset
series.releasePattern: New working papers released weekly at nber.org; AI-labor subset roughly monthly
series.topicLine: The single feed where the field's causal-identification AI-labor papers originate.
series.whatItMeasures: Not a data series — a working-paper feed. Where Brynjolfsson/Chandar/Chen (Canaries), Humlum/Vestergaard (Still Waters), Autor/Thompson (Expertise), Manning/Aguirre (adaptive capacity), Acemoglu (Simple Macro of AI + Pro-Worker AI), and Bick/Blandin/Deming (RPS) all publish first.
series.whyItMatters: Every ingested Tier 1 paper on the site traces back to this feed. Tracking NBER weekly is how the site stays ahead of Fed / IMF / OECD syntheses (which lag academic publication by 3-9 months). This is where the 'first inning' research Kolko flags is being written.

lastIngested.value: Latest ingested AI-labor NBER WP: Chen/Sialm/Xu on AI in asset management (Jun 2026). ~9 NBER WPs ingested since March 2026

series.nextExpected: Continuous — NBER releases new AI-labor WPs nearly weekly; check for new titles at least monthly

series.name: ILO — AI and the Future of Work / Global Employment Trends
series.cadenceLabel: Annual Global Report + interim policy notes
series.releasePattern: Director-General's annual report at International Labour Conference (June); interim thematic notes throughout the year
series.topicLine: The only worker-voice and decent-work framing in the AI-labor registry.
series.whatItMeasures: Global employment status, informality, decent-work indicators tied to AI adoption. The 2026 Director-General's report 'A Moment of Choice: Harnessing AI for Decent Work' is the anchor artifact. ILO-World Bank joint paper series adds cross-country generative-AI exposure estimates.
series.whyItMatters: Every other source on the registry frames AI-labor as a productivity/displacement question. ILO frames it as a decent-work + worker-voice question — the framing Kinder pushes and the framing that maps to policy conversations in most OECD countries. Also: 2.1 billion workers in informal employment are outside the US-focused datasets entirely.

lastIngested.value: 'A Moment of Choice' DG report: AI transforms tasks not occupations; jobs gap 408M in 2026

series.name: IFR World Robotics Report
series.releasePattern: Full report September each year; press-release Top-5 Trends in January
series.topicLine: The definitive global source on industrial robot installations by country, sector, and application.
series.whatItMeasures: Industrial robot installations and operational stock by country, industry, and application. Covers cobots, service robots, and mobile robots. Data underlies Acemoglu-Restrepo's JPE 2020 finding that one more robot per thousand workers reduces employment-to-population by 0.2pp.
series.whyItMatters: The physical-automation counterweight to a site dominated by GenAI/knowledge-work signals. Robotics adoption is real, measurable, and directly implicated in manufacturing employment. Feeds robots-physical-automation-displacement — currently the thinnest displacement graph on the site.

lastIngested.value: Global robot installations +6% to 575K units in 2025; US +11% to 38K units

series.name: Anthropic Economic Index Dashboard (base data)
series.cadenceLabel: Continuous dashboard; updated with each themed report
series.releasePattern: Dashboard at anthropic.com/economic-index; refreshed with each quarterly report
series.topicLine: Task-level automation-vs-augmentation ratios by O*NET occupation — the input Stanford Canaries analysis relies on.
series.whatItMeasures: Analysis of millions of Claude conversations mapped to O*NET occupations, classifying each usage as automation or augmentation. Different from the individual themed reports (Learning Curves, Cadences, 81K Economics) already on the registry — this is the underlying dashboard artifact that Brynjolfsson/Chandar/Chen and others use as the 'how is AI actually used?' input.
series.whyItMatters: The single largest AI usage dataset in the field. Stanford DEL Canaries analysis uses the automation ratio here to explain why early-career workers in automation-heavy occupations contract 3.8%/yr while augmentation-heavy occupations grow. Rock and Brynjolfsson both cite this as the key input for measuring how (not just whether) AI is deployed at the task level.

lastIngested.value: Dashboard updated with each themed report; latest: Cadences (June 2026)
